say: The Mongols took Tahng Long, the capital of Die Vee-et, three times: in twelve fifty-eight, in twelve eighty-five, and again in twelve eighty-eight.
Each time, they had to leave. In the end, they never held the kingdom of Die Vee-et.
Why not? The answer is not one heroic battle. It is strategy, supply, climate and politics. Let's see what each side's records say.
By the twelve fifties, the Mongols ruled from northern China to Persia. In twelve fifty-eight, another Mongol army sacked Baghdad.
Their great unfinished war was against the Song dynasty, which still held southern China.
During that war, Mongol armies had already conquered the kingdom of Dah-lee, in today's Yoon-nahn, in the early twelve fifties.
South of Yoon-nahn lay Die Vee-et, ruled by the Chun dynasty from Tahng Long, today's Hanoi.
For the Mongols, Die Vee-et lay on the southern edge of their campaigns. For the Chun, the Mongols were a new power on the border.
Late in twelve fifty-seven, the Mongol general Oo-ree-yang-ka-dye marched down from Yoon-nahn toward the Red River.
It was not a huge army. Estimates differ, but historians speak of a few thousand Mongols, with larger numbers of troops raised in Yoon-nahn.
He won a battle against the Chun army and took Tahng Long. The king and his court escaped.
The Yuan official history says the Mongols stayed just nine days, and left because of the heat.
Modern historians add the bigger picture: this was a side front in the war on the Song.
Soon after, the Chun sent envoys and agreed to pay tribute. Round one ended in a deal, not a victory parade.
In twelve sixty, Koo-bly became Great Khan. In twelve seventy-one he proclaimed a new dynasty in China: the Yuan.
In twelve sixty-one he recognised the Chun ruler as King of Ahn-nahm. Then, in twelve sixty-seven, he asked for much more.
The Yuan history lists six demands. The king must come to court in person, send his sons as hostages, and count his people.
He must also supply soldiers, pay taxes, and accept a Mongol overseer, called a dah-roo-gah-chee.
The Chun sent envoys and gifts. But no Chun king made the journey north to Koo-bly's court.
The Yuan history treats this as a vassal's defiance. Later Vietnamese histories frame the refusals as resistance. Same facts, two readings.
Meanwhile, in the early twelve eighties, a Yuan army attacked Champa, Die Vee-et's neighbour to the south.
The Vietnamese chronicle says that in twelve eighty-four the Chun reviewed their troops, and the retired king called village elders to ask their counsel.
According to the chronicle, the elders all answered: fight. It is a famous scene, but it comes from one side's record only.
The defence was led by Prince Chun Kwok Twun, better known as Chun Hung Dow.
Vietnamese tradition also credits him with a fiery proclamation to his officers, though its exact date and wording are uncertain.
Early in twelve eighty-five, the Yuan struck. Koo-bly's son Toe-gahn came from the north. So-geh-too marched up from Champa.
How big was the army? Modern estimates run from tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand. The Vietnamese chronicle claims half a million. Nobody knows for sure.
The Chun lost the first battles. The court abandoned Tahng Long, and the Yuan moved into empty palaces.
Some of the royal family went over to the Yuan. Prince Chun Ick Tuck surrendered, and Koo-bly later named him King of Ahn-nahm.
Another defector, Lay Tuck, later wrote a history of Ahn-nahm in exile in China. It gives us a third view of this war.
Then the tide turned. Chun forces struck back along the rivers, and So-geh-too was killed.
By mid-twelve eighty-five, after the Chun counter-attacks, the Yuan armies had pulled back north.
Koo-bly did not give up. In late twelve eighty-seven the Yuan came back, and by early twelve eighty-eight they held Tahng Long for the third time.
This time, food for the army would come by sea, on a fleet of grain ships.
The Chun did what they had done before. They left the capital, and kept their army out of reach.
Then the Chun general Chun Kahn Zuh caught the grain fleet. The Vietnamese chronicle says the ships were almost all overturned.
The Yuan history tells it differently: its commander dumped the rice into the sea and sailed away to Hainan.
Either way, the result was the same. The army in Tahng Long had too little to eat.
The Yuan history records the generals' worry: the weather was already hot, the grain was running out, and the army was worn down.
So they decided to withdraw. The army would leave by land, and the fleet by river, down the Bahk Dahng.
The Bahk Dahng is a tidal river near the coast. In nine thirty-eight, Ngoh Kwee-en had defeated a Southern Han fleet there, using stakes in the riverbed.
Three and a half centuries later, another battle on the Bahk Dahng would use stakes again.
According to the Vietnamese chronicle, Chun Hung Dow had wooden stakes planted in the riverbed and covered with grass.
At high tide, the stakes were hidden under water. The Yuan fleet came down the river.
When the tide fell, the ships were caught on the stakes. Smaller Chun boats closed in.
The Vietnamese chronicle says the Yuan fleet suffered heavy losses. It claims hundreds of ships were taken, and the admiral Omar was captured and brought before the retired king.
On land, Toe-gahn's army retreated north under attack, all the way to the border.
Archaeologists have since found wooden stakes in old riverbeds in the area. How many belong to the battle of twelve eighty-eight is still debated.
So did Die Vee-et beat the Mongols? Yes, and no. The Yuan withdrew. But the Chun quickly sent envoys to make peace.
They sent tribute, and a golden figure in place of the king. The Yuan history says it was to stand in for his guilt.
Koo-bly still planned another invasion in twelve ninety-three. After he died in twelve ninety-four, his successor ordered the campaign stopped.
Die Vee-et was not alone. Koo-bly's fleets also failed against Japan, in twelve seventy-four and twelve eighty-one, and against Java in the early twelve nineties.
So why couldn't the Yuan hold Die Vee-et? Read side by side, the records point to the same few things.
An enemy that gave up its capital but not its army. Supply lines that could be cut. The heat. And for Koo-bly, this was one war among many.
The Yuan records describe a disobedient vassal that finally sent tribute. Vietnamese histories celebrate three victories, and Chun Hung Dow, later worshipped as a saint.
Which side's record do you trust more? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to Rice and Empires for more.
